newsitem.title: USA: House lawmakers to speed cereal price report.
newsitem.headline: House lawmakers to speed cereal price report.

text.p: A pair of House lawmakers said Thursday they plan to push up the release of an annual report on breakfast cereal prices after a major cereal maker said this week it was boosting prices.

General Mills Corp., the U.S.'s second largest cereal maker, said on Wednesday it was raising its cereal prices by an average of 2.6 percent. The move made General Mills the first major cereal maker to boost prices since a round of industry price cuts last year.
General Mills said it took the action to adjust for inflation. But Representative Sam Gejdenson, a Connecticut Democrat, on Thursday accused the company of "playing games with consumers.

"Their 11 percent price reduction, announced last June, applied to less than half of their cereal products," Gedjenson said in a statement. It also excluded Cheerios and Wheaties, two of their best-selling brands, he said.

The General Mills price hike was not likely to prompt legislation, but it has accelerated plans by Gedjenson and Representative Charles Schumer, a New York Democrat, to release their third annual report on cereal industry pricing practices.

The thrust of third Gedjenson-Schumer report will be that cereal manufacturers have benefited more from the favourable publicity of cutting cereal prices than consumers have from lower prices, a Gedjenson aide said.
The report should be out in two to three weeks, he said.

Gedjenson has been on a crusade against what he regards as excessively high cereal prices since 1994, when he noticed on a shopping trip with his children that some cereal was priced at close to $5 a box, the aide said.
Shortly after the second Gedjenson-Schumer report last year, Post Cereal cut its cereal prices by 20 percent.
That action by Post, owned by Philip Morris Cos. Inc., prompted General Mills, Kellogg Co. and Quaker Oats Co. to cut prices.
Following General Mills' price increase analysts said they were watching to see if the company follows with an increase in discount coupon offers.

That was the pattern in the industry in the early 1990s, when the companies would raise prices, then try to attract consumers with discounts. But that has changed in recent years, with cereal companies cutting prices, but also cutting back on promotional spending.
Industry leader Kellogg would not say if it would follow General Mills' lead in raising prices. Quaker and Post Cereals also had no comment.

"My guess at this point is the whole industry would go for a price increase," said Nomi Ghez at Goldman Sachs. She said Kellogg might raise prices on selected brands, while Post and Quaker Oats would be likely to raise prices across the board.
